name: Ben Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: The Work Futures Panel is independent and has no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Ben Weber, 43, a senior haul-truck operator at a large mine. I check the brakes, read the ramp conditions, and move loads; I use AI every day to compare fuel figures, but I still make the call from the cab.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what is hard at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like adjusting a route when a ramp is slower than the plan. My partner Sienna runs a small fishing charter, we have two school-age children and a mortgage, and our reserve covers about four months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say small software can clear the haul queue, but the driver still has to judge the ramp. I use an AI tool to compare fuel use with loads, and a person still has to check the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my shift is in the truck, and wages stay much as they were in this picture. My partner Sienna runs a fishing charter, so her income rises and falls with bookings; we keep four months of bills in reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the truck checks and test the queue planner against the dispatch radio for two weeks. I would leave the reserve untouched until the mine actually changed my hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the truck job in this mild picture. I know the charter has quiet weeks, but that is an old budget issue, not a new AI shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your partner to check first if your pay changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask Sienna to compare the next charter bookings with our mortgage date. We could delay repainting the porch before using money set aside for the children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029, 2032 or 2037 after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the queue suggestions with the ramp schedule and fuel records. If the tool gives a sensible order for several weeks, I would keep checking its work rather than trust it blindly.

I use AI to compare **fuel use** with loads.
think: Most of my day is in the **truck**, and wages stay steady here.
I rely on my four-month **reserve** when charter bookings slow.
do: Keep the truck checks and compare the **queue planner** with radio calls.
Leave the **reserve** untouched until the mine changes my hours.
feel: I feel **calm** about the truck job, though the charter has quiet weeks.
S0.quote: I would say small software can clear the haul queue, but the driver still has to judge the ramp.
fieldNote: Ben already uses AI for **fuel comparisons**, but verifies every result.
His partner’s seasonal charter income explains why the **reserve** matters.
The plateau leaves his own mining role relatively **steady**.

steps.text: Check AI fuel comparisons against actual truck loads
Keep the haul truck checks on each shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the software will take more booking and route planning first. A shift sheet cannot show a loose rock beside the ramp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead work includes allocating trucks and comparing haul times, so some of my screen hours could go. I still spend most shifts driving, and I have not decided whether I would want fewer lead duties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would volunteer for a month-long trial of the new route tool and learn how to question its fuel estimate. I would ask the mine to price a drill-and-blast support course before I signed up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because the data tools are easy for me, but a crew cut would still change the family budget. I do not think the truck disappears in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your partner to check first if your pay changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the other senior drivers to log where the software sends trucks into a delay. Then I could show dispatch specific examples instead of arguing from a hunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029, 2032 or 2037 after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want two weeks of route recommendations compared with real ramp conditions before changing my routine. If the tool misses a stoppage, I would keep the radio check.

S1.quote: A shift sheet cannot show a loose rock beside the ramp.
fieldNote: His AI exposure is concentrated in truck assignment and **haul planning**.
Ben does not assume that screen work remains a **career** after AGI.
He wants site data to test the software before changing field **routines**.

steps.text: Test the route tool against ramp conditions
Ask for the cost of the drill-and-blast support course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell people the mine’s reports and dispatch can change by 2028, while loader robots come around 2031. The three-year gap is time to qualify for other field work, not a promise of a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could take my allocations and haul reports quickly, and robots could take the driving work after that. I use AI every day, but I cannot see a screen-based job as protection from a thinking machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the training office now about a recognized drill-and-blast support qualification. In 2029, I would take the mine-paid course while keeping my truck shifts, then apply for a field support opening if one was posted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fast date makes me anxious because the truck is most of my income. Four months saved and some nearby mines give me options, but I would not count on a permanent place in field support.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your partner to check first if your pay changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sienna and I would check the course timetable against her charter season and the mortgage. I would only spend on travel if the mine confirmed the course was paid and the opening was real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029, 2032 or 2037 after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no course ran in 2029, I would keep driving and ask the blasting crew to let me observe a planned support shift. I would not borrow for an outside certificate before checking local vacancies.

do: Ask now for the recognized drill-and-blast **qualification**.
Take the paid course in 2029 while keeping my **truck shifts**.

S2.quote: I cannot see a screen-based job as protection from a thinking machine.
fieldNote: Ben separates daily AI use from protection against full **AGI**.
He seeks a specific field credential and applies only if there is an **opening**.

steps.text: Take the mine-paid drill-and-blast support course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets us prepare before AGI arrives in 2031, with robots reaching truck work around 2034. The mine should publish which field roles it expects to staff after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The haul reports may go first, while the truck gives me another three years. Drill-and-blast support is a route to test, but robots may eventually handle parts of that work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take the qualification over the next few years and ask to shadow a blasting crew during a planned shift. In 2032, I would apply for a funded support role if the work still needed a person on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the later robot date, even though five years gives me time to train. I would not leave a paid job for a certificate that leads nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your partner to check first if your pay changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask whether the support role means field setup, safety checks or mostly digital reporting. I want to know what a person does on the ground before I choose that course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029, 2032 or 2037 after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2032, I would inspect the actual job description and ask how often the crew uses automated equipment. If the work is mostly reports, I would keep driving and check other local sites.

say: I see five years to prepare before AGI in **2031**.
I would ask which field roles remain after robots arrive around **2034**.
think: I expect haul reports to go first, while truck work may last **three years**.
Drill support is only a route to test, not lasting **protection**.
do: Take the field **qualification** and shadow the blasting crew.
Apply in 2032 for a funded role with **on-site work**.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though five years gives me time to train carefully.
S3.quote: Drill-and-blast support is a route to test, but robots may eventually handle parts of that work too.
fieldNote: He explores field support while acknowledging later **robot exposure**.
Ben wants a job description that distinguishes field tasks from **reporting**.
He would keep driving if no funded on-site **vacancy** exists.

steps.text: Apply for a funded on-site support role in 2032
Keep driving until a field offer is confirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew a decade gives us time if the mine shares real dates. Thinking work changes in 2036, and robots may reach truck driving around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 when AGI arrives and 56 when robots follow, and I will still need earnings. I could try a field qualification, but I would keep checking whether that work is being automated too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would finish the support qualification while staying on my truck rota and put a fixed amount of each wage into savings. In 2037, I would apply for a site-support post only if it had funded hours and real field work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer warning makes the change easier to plan around. I still feel uneasy about the work after 2039, because a course cannot guarantee the mine will keep a crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask your partner to check first if your pay changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2037, the children will be young adults, and Sienna and I would ask what training they want before helping with a course. I would point them toward skills that work outside the mine and charter business too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2029, 2032 or 2037 after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the next staffing dates and compare support vacancies at two nearby mines. I would only move the family after a signed offer covered the mortgage and travel costs.

say: I see a decade to prepare if the mine shares **real dates**.
I expect thinking work to change by 2036 and truck robots to follow around **2039**.
think: At 53 and 56, I will still need **earnings**.
I would keep checking whether field support is also being **automated**.
do: Finish field training while keeping my **truck rota**.
Save part of my wage and apply for funded site support in **2037**.
feel: The longer warning helps me plan, but I remain **uneasy** about work after 2039.
S4.quote: I still feel uneasy about the work after 2039, because a course cannot guarantee the mine will keep a crew.
fieldNote: Ben keeps earning while pursuing **field training**.
He expects his children to be young adults by **2037** and includes them in course choices.
He would move only if a signed offer covered family **costs**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because planning could go before I am ready for the truck robots. A recognized course, funded field work and enough notice to plan with Sienna would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would want managers to show which course leads to an actual job and what the work involves. I can learn quickly, but I will not mistake a certificate for a guarantee.

headlineQuote: I will not mistake a certificate for a guarantee.
portrait: Ben is a 43-year-old senior mine operator with a **technical diploma**.
He uses AI daily to compare fuel figures and checks its results against **field conditions**.
His partner runs a fishing charter; they have a mortgage and **four months saved**.
He is willing to train for field work but expects **robots** may automate parts of it too.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries him because dispatch work changes before he can qualify for field support.
whatWouldHelp: A recognized **course**, funded field work and clear notice would help Ben plan with Sienna.
